blocks.text: III. The Mind of Evil Stirring Without Rest

inline.s: Zhang said, “I have known what happens in your home for a long time. Your mind of evil is far too heavy, and you pursue only empty reputation. Your pages are full of complaint and resentment, and you lay these before the Lord on High — I fear the punishment due you will not stop here.”

The gentleman was greatly alarmed and said, “I have heard that in the invisible realm not the smallest good deed goes unrecorded. I have sworn to do good and have long observed your rules — how can it all be empty reputation?”

Zhang said, “Take, for instance, the rule about cherishing the written word. Your pupils and close friends often use old writings and books to paper their windows and wrap things, even to wipe the table, yet they make the excuse of not letting them be soiled and burn them. You see this daily and never say a single word of admonition — but when you find a scrap of written paper on the road, you pick it up and put it to the fire. What good is that?”

“Each month the association releases living creatures. You hurry along with the crowd and let others do the work. If the others did not act, you too would merely drift. In truth, the thought of compassion has never stirred within you.”
“And as for the shrimp and crabs in your own household — they too come to the kitchen board. You abstain from killing, yet are they not also living beings?”

“As to the fault of speech: you are quick and clever with words, and listeners are often won over by you. At the moment you speak, you know in your heart that you wound others, yet in the familiar talk among friends you mock and laugh with the tide and cannot stop yourself. Whatever your sharp tongue reaches, it provokes the anger of spirits. The tally of your secret evil is beyond counting, yet still you pose as simple and virtuous. Whom are you deceiving? Are you deceiving Heaven?”

“As to lust, though there has been no real act: when you see a handsome boy or girl, you stare fixedly, and your heart is shaken and cannot put the image away — only, no illicit chance happens to meet! Reflect on yourself: placed in such a situation, could you conduct yourself like the chaste man of Lu? Yet you claim that all your life you have been free of lust, and so may face Heaven, Earth, gods and spirits — this is truly self-deception!”
“If this is how matters stand with the very rules you have sworn to practice, how much the more so with the rest.”

“The memorials you have burned for years have all been laid before Heaven. The Lord on High has commanded the Messenger Who Travels by Day to observe your good and evil for several years, and not a single good deed can be recorded. But in your private, solitary moments, we see your greedy thoughts, lustful thoughts, envious thoughts, mean-spirited thoughts, self-exalting and others-belittling thoughts, thoughts dwelling on the past and hoping for the future, thoughts of repaying kindness and avenging wrongs — churning endlessly within you, beyond all counting. These manifold evils of the mind have taken root within you; the spirits have recorded them in abundance, and Heaven’s punishment grows heavier day by day. You can hardly escape calamity — how could you beg for blessing?”

The gentleman, startled and terrified, prostrated himself on the ground weeping and said, “Since you understand the hidden realm, you must surely be a venerable deity. I beg your help and deliverance.”

Zhang said, “You read books and understand propriety, and you know that delighting in goodness is a pleasure. When you hear a good word, you are stirred to exhortation; when you see a good deed, you are full of inspiration. Yet it is gone as soon as it passes, for your root of faith was never deep, and your constancy is therefore unstable. All your good words and deeds through life have been perfunctory and drifting; never once have you done anything real. Presently your heart is filled with evils of mind rising and falling, and still you demand a fine reward from Heaven — it is like planting thorns over all the ground and foolishly hoping to harvest fine grain. Is this not absurd!”

“From this day on, whatever greedy, lustful, angry, and deluded stray thoughts arise, first drive them all out with all your might, and keep your mind clean and pure — let every single thought attend only to the good. If a good deed lies within your strength, do it without expecting return, without seeking fame, regardless of its size or difficulty — steadily, concretely, with patience. If it is beyond your strength, still be diligent and earnest, so that the good intention may come to fullness. First, you must have patience; second, you must have an enduring mind. Never be lazy, never deceive yourself. Do this for a long while, and there will be unfathomable results.”

“You have served me in my household with great reverence and purity, and I tell you this in return. Hasten to practice diligently, and you may turn back Heaven’s will.” When he finished, he went at once into the inner chamber. The gentleman rose and followed him, until at the stove he suddenly vanished. Only then did he realize that it had been the God of the Stove, the ruler of destiny; so he burned incense and bowed in thanks.

On New Year’s Day of the following year, he bowed and prayed to Heaven and Earth, swore to reform his past faults, and truly practiced good deeds. He changed his own sobriquet, calling himself “the Daoist of Purified Intent,” as a vow to put away all delusions.

On the first days of the practice, stray thoughts assailed him in crowds; now he doubted, now he was lax, and the days passed while he drifted as before. So before the image of the Great Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara kept in his family shrine, he knocked his head to the ground until it bled and made a solemn vow: “May my good thoughts remain forever pure and my power of good advance; if I give myself the slightest indulgence, may I fall forever into hell.” Every morning he devoutly recited the holy name of the Great Compassionate One a hundred times, to pray for unseen aid.

From then on, whether in speech or in deed, in a single thought or a single moment, he was as though the gods and spirits stood at his side, and he dared not be negligent or wanton. Whatever could benefit others or help living things — great or small, in leisure or in haste, seen or unseen, sustained or unavailing — he performed it with joy, bending all his effort to bring it to completion. Following conditions and using every means, he broadly planted hidden merit. He also urged upon all he met the duties of human relations, diligence in study, humility, forbearance, and the words of cause and effect and retribution, ever fearing his days were not enough. At the end of each month he summed up what he had done and said, and wrote a memorial laid before the God of the Stove.
When his practice had become well-established, in movement ten thousand good deeds followed him, and in stillness not a single thought arose. Thus for three years.

blocks.text: VI. Storing Blessing to Turn Heaven’s Mind

inline.s: At the age of fifty — which was the second year of the Wanli reign, the jiaxu examination year — the metropolitan examination was held. Zhang Jiangling was the first grand secretary, and after the examination closed he sought out fellow townsmen to choose a tutor for his son. Everyone praised the gentleman with one voice, and so he was engaged and summoned to the capital, and the gentleman brought his family along. Zhang respected his virtue and character and secured his entry into the Imperial College by precedent. In the fourth year of Wanli, bingzi, he sat the capital provincial examination and passed, and the next year he became a palace graduate.

One day he called on the eunuch Mr. Yang, who had his five adopted sons come out to bow to him. Yang had searched all four directions for them, to be his heirs and please his old age. Among them was a boy of sixteen whose face seemed familiar to the gentleman. He asked where he was from, and the boy said, “I am from Jiangyou. When small, I was taken by mistake onto a grain boat; I still dimly recall my surname and my district.” The gentleman was very surprised and had him take off his left shoe: two moles were plainly there. He cried out, “This is my son!” Yang too was astonished, and at once sent the boy back with the gentleman to his lodging. He ran to tell his wife. The mother embraced the boy and wept bitterly, like blood and tears bursting forth. The boy also wept, held his mother’s face and licked her eyes — and her two eyes recovered their sight.

The gentleman was filled with grief and joy at once. He no longer wished to be an official, and declined the post to return home. Zhang, admiring his righteousness, showered him with generous gifts and let him go. Living in the countryside, he did good deeds all the more zealously. His son took a wife and in succession had seven sons, all of whom were raised and all carried on the family’s scholarly tradition.

The gentleman wrote out with his own hand the account of meeting the God of the Stove and of truly reforming his faults, to instruct his descendants. He enjoyed a life of robust health, living to eighty-eight. People all said that this was the reward of truly doing good and turning back Heaven’s will.
Recorded by Luo Zhen, a younger scholar and fellow townsman.
